idiom_name: one module per table + record-set parameters
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: create one module per table or view and give it the procedures that act on all rows of that table, taking and returning record sets (row collections plus their column metadata) rather than per-row objects. Keep the SQL in a data-access object (Table Data Gateway) that the module calls; the module holds rules, the gateway holds statements. Keep the module stateless so a single instance (or, in languages without instances, a package or translation unit) can be shared, and let callers own the transaction boundary: multi-table use cases belong in a Service Layer that wraps the module calls in one transaction. Express rules as set operations (bulk update/insert, aggregate query) whenever the database can do them, and iterate rows only for rules the query language cannot express.
pitfalls: Letting the module own connections or transactions: the boundary belongs above it (Service Layer), otherwise multi-table use cases commit partially.
Fetching a whole table into memory and looping per row instead of issuing one set-oriented statement; the pattern's benefit is the set pass, not the loop.
Letting the module grow into a god class: once a table's rules stop forming a coherent unit, split by use case or move the object-shaped parts to a richer model.
Returning raw record sets to presentation code that mutates them, bypassing the module's rules.

Set-oriented bulk writes bypassing per-row hooks: Rails update_all and Django QuerySet.update() skip validations, callbacks and save() by design, so rules that live on the row model go unenforced - encode such rules in the statement itself or in database constraints.

Mixing set-oriented writes with already-loaded row objects leaves the identity map and any in-memory record set stale; refresh or discard loaded rows after a bulk update, or commit to one path per use case.
